title: a lineage
hook: who taught your teacher's teacher? an Upanishad names the chain, and a letter of Paul's looks ahead
tomorrow: why would an Upanishad stop to list its teachers' names?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the graduate's path met a new teacher the Gita's way: bow, ask, serve. Today, the people behind that teacher.

Ask someone who taught them a family recipe and the answer starts running backward. My aunt. Well, she got it from her mother-in-law. Who got it from a neighbor back home, maybe. Every skill you have came through a chain of hands. So: who taught your teacher's teacher? The Mundaka Upanishad opens by answering that question for itself.
screen: `A RECIPE, RUNNING BACKWARD.` → `A CHAIN OF HANDS.` → `WHO TAUGHT YOUR TEACHER?`

segments.voice: Its first lines name a lineage. Brahma, first of the gods, maker of all, taught the knowledge of Brahman to Atharvan, his eldest son. Atharvan told it to Angir. Angir to Satyavaha, of the Bharadvaja family. He handed it to Angiras. Then a householder named Shaunaka comes to Angiras, the right way, and asks: what is it that, once known, makes all this known? The chain exists so that question can be asked. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words. In the New Testament, Paul writes to a younger man, Timothy: "the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also." The same letter remembers the faith that lived first in Timothy's grandmother Lois. Shared: a teaching passes person to person, and the passing is part of the teaching. And an honest difference. The Mundaka names its chain backward, all the way up to Brahma, and the knowledge is of Brahman. Paul's chain runs forward to people not yet named, and what's handed on is the message about Jesus. One looks up the line; one looks down it. Both put a person at each link.
screen: `BRAHMA, ATHARVAN, ANGIR...` · `SHAUNAKA ASKS.` · `PAUL: TEACH OTHERS ALSO.` · `BACKWARD, AND FORWARD.`

segments.voice: Say aloud, softly, the name of one person who taught you something you still use. Then, if you know it, the name of the person who taught them. Let each name sit in the air for a breath before the next.
A lineage: a teaching passed person to person. The Mundaka names its chain back to Brahma; a letter of Paul's hands it forward.
Keep this: a lineage. Every link in it has a name, even the ones we've forgotten.

chat.meaning: The Mundaka names its chain back to Brahma; 2 Timothy hands it forward to those who'll teach others. Shared: person to person. Different: what's handed on.

Mundaka.meaning: an Upanishad that opens by naming its line of teachers

Brahma.meaning: the creator god, first in the Mundaka's chain

Atharvan.meaning: Brahma's eldest son, second in the chain

Shaunaka.meaning: a householder who brings his question to Angiras

Timothy.meaning: a younger companion of Paul, to whom Paul wrote letters

notes: Wisdom shape, unity thread: shared with Christianity, in its own words and source (2 Timothy 2:2, KJV): a teaching handed person to person, the handing part of the teaching. Honest difference: the Mundaka names its chain backward to Brahma and hands on knowledge of Brahman; Paul's letter looks forward to people not yet named and hands on the message about Jesus. Never 'the same'; neither ranked; the chat's wrong option 'mean the same thing' is the skimmer's pick.

KJV 2 Timothy 2:2 opens 'And the things...'; the quotation starts at 'the things'. 2 Timothy 1:5 also names Timothy's mother Eunice; the script names only the grandmother, Lois, to fit the storyline (Priya's mother has died; nothing stands in for her). Confirm.
Pauline authorship of 2 Timothy is debated among scholars; the script says 'Paul writes', as the letter itself does. Confirm that framing is acceptable.
Mundaka 1.2.12 was used yesterday (fuel in hand); today is 1.1.1–3. Gita 4.1–3's chain is held for 1787.
